skyline.text: The state should be leg­i­ble to us, says Amit Varma
Ajay Shah calls neat plan­ta­tions ig­no­rance dressed up as sci­ence
Newton’s gra­cious line was re­ally a jab at Robert Hooke

masthead.footnote: *So you think seeing is free. Actually, seeing is very hard. Page 2

brief.head: Pass the baton
brief.text: Change comes through a relay of ideas, Ajay Shah said. Short-termists cheer the last run­ner; you have to see ev­ery­one who handed the baton up­stream. {115-C01}

brief.head: After the Wall fell
brief.text: Once the USSR col­lapsed, Ajay Shah said, many in democ­ra­cies drifted to­wards tech­no­cratic so­cial en­gi­neer­ing. “Now that the USSR is gone, let’s be a lit­tle bit more like the USSR.” {115-C02}

brief.head: Delete by default
brief.text: When you pay a toll, the state learns where your car was. Ajay Shah wants such data deleted within sec­onds un­less the peo­ple au­tho­rise keep­ing it. {115-C07}

brief.head: Safe in Norway
brief.text: Electronic pay­ments are rea­son­ably safe in Norway and a prison in North Korea, Ajay Shah said. How much a state may see should de­pend on its free­doms. {115-C15}

brief.head: A thousand Singapores
brief.text: India is a thou­sand Singapore-sized lo­cales, Ajay Shah said, so one ruler in­struct­ing all of it is “a recipe for trou­ble”. {#locales}

thought.who: Amit Varma, admitting that Chandigarh’s wide roads and clean air hide a price

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on James C Scott’s classic
lead.head: The state that can’t see the trees

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 115

body: Amit Varma opened with a rock band. Only thirty peo­ple bought the Velvet Underground’s al­bums, it was once said, and all thirty be­came mu­si­cians. James C Scott, he ar­gued, is the Velvet Underground of ideas. {115-J12}
Mention Scott in pub­lic and peo­ple say “James who?”, Varma said. Yet he is “a dom­i­nant in­flu­ence on many oth­ers who are dom­i­nant in­flu­ences on the world at large”.
The episode was given over to Scott’s *Seeing Like a State*, the 1998 book that changed Ajay Shah’s life. Its sub­ti­tle asks why cer­tain schemes to im­prove the human con­di­tion have failed.

Some of the smartest peo­ple in the world, Shah said, led such schemes. P C Mahalanobis was a great physi­cist and a great statis­ti­cian. “And yet when it came to think­ing about so­ci­ety, his stuff was phe­nom­e­nally wrong.” {115-C03}
## Three tools
Shah set out the book as a tool­kit of three ideas.

The first is state leg­i­bil­ity. A per­son sees with­out ef­fort; a state sees only when an of­fi­cial writes some­thing on file, with all the dis­cre­tion, bribery and se­crecy that in­vites. So states force peo­ple to be­come eas­ier to read, with con­se­quences no­body in­tended.

The sec­ond is high mod­ernism, “the be­lief that sci­en­tists and en­gi­neers have a su­pe­rior claim upon knowl­edge about so­ci­ety”, im­posed from the top by the co­er­cive power of the state. {115-C08}
The third is metis: local, tacit knowl­edge gained by doing, which can­not be writ­ten into a man­ual and which changes if you move a hun­dred kilo­me­tres.
## A for­est made count­able

Scott’s cen­tral ex­am­ple is Prussian sci­en­tific forestry, which Shah said is just as much the story of British forestry in India. The for­est is re­duced to one aim, tim­ber, and re­planted as a mono­cul­ture in clean rows.
It is easy to count and easy to kill. One in­sect or one fun­gus can wipe it out, and the soil is de­graded. “This is ig­no­rance. It’s not sci­ence,” Shah said. {115-C10}

Things go worst, Scott ar­gues, when four el­e­ments meet: a high-modernist phi­los­o­phy, state power used to make so­ci­ety leg­i­ble, an au­thor­i­tar­ian state and a civil so­ci­ety too weak to push back.

Shah’s ex­am­ples ran from Stalin’s col­lec­tive farms to Brasília, Bombay’s Bandra Kurla Complex and India’s Green Revolution. Varma con­fessed that he was born in Chandigarh, a city de­signed by “one of the vil­lains of high mod­ernism”.
## Humility, not abo­li­tion
Scott does not want the state to wither away, Shah said. We need a mo­nop­oly of vi­o­lence, law and order and mon­e­tary pol­icy. The mes­sage is hu­mil­ity: make small moves that can be un­done.
“The state has a lust for ar­bi­trary power,” he said, just as firms lust for profit. So every new way for the state to see must come with com­men­su­rate checks and bal­ances.
Varma turned the ques­tion around. “We don’t need to be leg­i­ble to them,” he said. “The state needs to be leg­i­ble to us.” {115-C06}

The tool­kit, Shah said, is an en­gine for think­ing about the world, well be­yond gov­ern­ments. He set lis­ten­ers a chal­lenge: take any episode of the show and write a com­ment on how it links to *Seeing Like a State*.
Varma took it up at once with the show’s cy­cling episode. What is a for­ma­tion of cy­clists in slip­stream, he asked, “if not high mod­ernism”?

second.label: Soviet collectivisation
second.head: Seeds sown in 1932
second.deck: Ajay Shah traces a 1991 vote and a Soviet collapse to Stalin’s farms

pic.caption: Official portrait of Joseph Stalin, issued for his 70th birthday in 1949

body: Stalin could be very prag­matic in some re­spects, Ajay Shah said. On col­lec­tivi­sa­tion he was “a bloody minded ide­o­logue”. When rich farm­ers re­sisted the state tak­ing their land, he crushed them with ex­treme bru­tal­ity.

In Ukraine, Stalin blocked off the food sup­ply and the Soviets grabbed the grain. Somewhere be­tween 4 and 10 per cent of Ukraine’s pop­u­la­tion died in a man-made famine. In 1991, Shah noted, 90 per cent of Ukraine voted to leave Russia. {115-S03}

The scheme cast a longer shadow. By the mid-80s, the Soviet econ­omy rested on ex­port­ing crude oil and im­port­ing grain. {#crude} When the price of crude fell and the price of grain rose, Shah said, the USSR col­lapsed.

quote.text: The seeds of the 1991 ref­er­en­dum where 90 per cent of Ukraine voted to leave Russia was sowed in 1932.

third.head: The number before the law

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Aadhaar and the privacy law

body: Ajay Shah was in the de­bates over Aadhaar. The first Aadhaar num­ber was is­sued in 2009, he said, on the un­der­stand­ing that a pri­vacy law was com­ing: Manmohan Singh’s gov­ern­ment was going to give it. {115-S04}
Then came Scott. Shah read *Seeing Like a State* only in 2012. “James C. Scott was slap­ping me around in 2012,” he said.
“Now I’m older and wiser,” Shah said. First show him the pri­vacy law, and a pow­er­ful one, match­ing “the dan­gers of a sin­gle num­ber that can be traced to every per­son in the coun­try”.

He added a pointed ob­ser­va­tion. Biometric ID sys­tems, he said, only hap­pen in poor, rel­a­tively au­thor­i­tar­ian de­vel­op­ing coun­tries, and not in ad­vanced democ­ra­cies. “I won­der why.” {#biometric}

p2.title: Reading the state
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s guide to James C Scott’s *Seeing Like a State*, from legibility to metis, argued over with Amit Varma. {115-R01}

from1.head: The state that can’t see the trees

quote.text: It’s the tech­no­cratic il­lu­sion that I’ll build a thou­sand man force and they’ll walk around the coun­try and they’ll see.

photo.caption: James C. Scott in 2016
photo.credit: SOAS University of London, CC BY 3.0

box.title: Scott, the Renaissance thinker
box.text: *Seeing Like a State* came out in 1998 and spans po­lit­i­cal phi­los­o­phy, so­ci­ol­ogy, an­thro­pol­ogy, urban pol­icy and de­vel­op­ment stud­ies. By then, Ajay Shah said, James C Scott was “a Renaissance thinker”, and field after field took to the book. {#renaissance}

sections.label: The first idea
sections.head: A bureaucracy has no eyes
sections.caption: state legibility
body: Seeing comes ef­fort­lessly to a human being, Ajay Shah said. A state is dif­fer­ent. “In a state, pol­icy is a map­ping from a state of na­ture to a state ac­tion”: an of­fi­cial must look, write some­thing on file, and only then does pol­icy kick in. {115-C04}
Every step is fraught: an official’s dis­cre­tion, the pull of a pro­mo­tion or a bribe, the sheer size of India, the shake­downs that fol­low when see­ing has con­se­quences, and se­crecy.
People hide, too. States have a grisly record of tax­a­tion, con­scrip­tion and en­slave­ment, Shah said, so peo­ple are not in­ter­ested in being seen.
## Flattening the fields
Shah’s pro­posed T-shirt slo­gan sums up what fol­lows: “State leg­i­bil­ity schemes have un­in­tended con­se­quences.” Amit Varma said it would come only in triple XL. {115-J03}

Land shows why. One per­son owns it, an­other has the right to grow the Kharif crop on it, and a third grazes cat­tle there when it lies fal­low. In a Burkean sense, Shah said, such ar­range­ments evolved for a rea­son.

A state that in­sists on one owner with all the rights is “a bull in a China shop”. Its logic is the Domesday Book’s: “if you have the land, I’ll tax you and I want clar­ity on who has the land.” {115-J15}
~ Varma would re­verse the flow. The state ex­ists to serve us, not rule us, he said, so it is the gov­ern­ment that should be ut­terly trans­par­ent and ac­count­able. {115-C06}

quote.text: It’s the tech­no­cratic il­lu­sion that I’ll build a thou­sand man force and they’ll walk around the coun­try and they’ll see.

sections.label: The second idea
sections.head: Not the same as modern
sections.caption: high modernism
body: When Amit Varma first heard the phrase high mod­ernism, he thought it meant “you wear shirt pant and you do drugs”. {115-J04}

Ajay Shah set him straight. Modernity is a good thing: sec­u­lar, in­di­vid­u­al­ist, free of su­per­sti­tion, with peo­ple deal­ing with one an­other as full per­sons rather than as kith, kin and tribe.
High mod­ernism is some­thing else. Varma com­pared the pair to pop­u­lar­ity and pop­ulism: “They’re al­most op­po­site things.” {115-J05}

It is, Shah said, “the be­lief that sci­en­tists and en­gi­neers have a su­pe­rior claim upon knowl­edge about so­ci­ety”, and that they should re­shape it through top-down schemes backed by the co­er­cion of the state. It stands for “one India, one X”. {115-C08}
## Why the schemes fail
Partly, the plan­ners lack the in­for­ma­tion. Partly, peo­ple re­spond to in­cen­tives: they hate the king, Shah said, and “smirk and smile” while qui­etly un­der­min­ing the grand scheme.
The high mod­ernist treats the past as an im­ped­i­ment to be swept away. Shah’s al­ter­na­tive is Burkean hu­mil­ity: make small moves, de­cen­tralise, rely on local knowl­edge.
~ India, he warned, is in a sec­ond wave of it, fed by the in­ter­net, tech bil­lion­aires, soft­ware suc­cess and a great re­gres­sion in po­lit­i­cal phi­los­o­phy. {#secondwave}

quote.text: High mod­ernism is this fan­tasy that there can be some cen­tralised rule and they will tell the peo­ple what to do.

sections.label: The third idea
sections.head: Knowledge you can’t write down
sections.caption: metis
body: The third idea is a word from Greek, which James C Scott im­ported into English: metis.

Scott sep­a­rates ob­jec­tive, uni­ver­sal knowl­edge, such as spe­cial rel­a­tiv­ity, from most knowl­edge about human so­ci­ety. That, Ajay Shah said, is metis: “deep ex­pe­ri­en­tial knowl­edge. It’s not knowl­edge in a book.” {115-C09}

You have to be there and do things to gain it. It is tacit: “once I ac­quire the knowl­edge, I can’t write it in a book and give it to you,” Shah said. And it is local, chang­ing from one place to the next.
## The op­po­site of a man­ual

Metis is not a sin­gle man­ual tossed down from above for ev­ery­one to fol­low. It car­ries judg­ment, hu­mil­ity and re­spect for how the world works. That makes it the exact op­po­site of high mod­ernism, which says: “We know this, we’ve read this book, we know how to do this. Now ev­ery­body fall in line.”

Shah car­ries the idea into busi­ness. He looks at the ar­ro­gance of a giant na­tional bank try­ing to run the whole bank through one process, one man­ual, and be­comes scep­ti­cal, be­cause “UP is not Maharashtra”. {#bank}
~ Amit Varma heard the same note in Jane Jacobs, whose work, he said, em­bod­ied an or­ganic ap­pre­ci­a­tion for spon­ta­neous order and for metis. {115-R15}

quote.text: It is very local knowl­edge. You move hun­dred kilo­me­tres the knowl­edge will change.

sections.label: The example
sections.head: The forest as a timber farm
sections.caption: Prussian scientific forestry
body: The ex­am­ple James C Scott uses in the book is Prussian sci­en­tific forestry. Ajay Shah said it is equally the story of British colo­nial forestry in India, and that it be­gins with an abuse of the word sci­ence. “Dude don’t pull the sci­ence card on me,” he said. {115-J06}
The for­est is taken to exist for one pur­pose: tim­ber. Foresters pick the tree that yields the most cubic me­tres a year and plant a mono­cul­ture in clean, or­derly rows.
At the Forest Research Institute in Dehradun, Shah said, ex­per­i­ments planted trees one metre or two me­tres apart, waited fifty years and counted the wood. {#forestry}
## A web, not a farm

A real for­est is many species, richly in­ter­con­nected and re­silient: an in­sect or a fun­gus kills a few things and the for­est is fine. The plan­ta­tion strips the soil of mi­cronu­tri­ents, and one in­sect or one fun­gus can de­stroy it all. {115-C10}

An in­spec­tor can count ex­actly a thou­sand trees. Legibility has been im­posed and the for­est de­stroyed. Explaining a joke, Shah said, is like dis­sect­ing a frog: “You can un­der­stand it, but it kills the frog.” {115-J14}
~ Amit Varma reached for Peter Wohlleben’s *The Hidden Life of Trees*, which made him re­alise that you can­not just plant forty trees to­gether and call it an ecosys­tem. {115-R17}

quote.text: When peo­ple in the world of pol­icy use the word sci­ence, you should start get­ting sus­pi­cious.

sections.label: The evidence
sections.head: From Daulatabad to Bandra
sections.caption: grand schemes that failed
body: Scott’s warn­ing is a four-part test, Ajay Shah said: a high-modernist phi­los­o­phy, state power used to ren­der so­ci­ety leg­i­ble, an au­thor­i­tar­ian state, and a civil so­ci­ety too weak to push back. “When you get these four things to­gether, you get ab­so­lutely bad out­comes.” {115-C11}

After Stalin’s farms, Shah turned to cities. There was “some bloke in Delhi” who thought of shift­ing the cap­i­tal to Daulatabad; there was Brasília. “Humans don’t re­spond to a cen­trally planned push to make a city.”
Bimal Patel’s rule, which Shah en­dorsed, is that 40 per cent of the land should be streets and parks, and peo­ple should de­cide the rest. {#patel}
Bombay’s Bandra Kurla Complex, sup­pos­edly a fi­nan­cial cen­tre, has tow­ers but no room for cof­fee shops. {#bkc}
## The Green Revolution, re­vis­ited

Shah ap­plied the same lens to the Green Revolution, which India re­mem­bers as its es­cape from PL 480. It was a top-down scheme of MSP, fer­tiliser sub­si­dies, free elec­tric­ity for pumps and a few cul­ti­vars of rice and wheat.

The longer bill in­cludes pes­ti­cides in the ground­wa­ter, re­gions of Punjab and Haryana filled with can­cer, and a ground­wa­ter cri­sis. The Netherlands, the area of Haryana, ex­ports $140 bil­lion of food. {#netherlands}
~ And the diet suf­fered. “We filled up the bel­lies of the peo­ple of India with starch,” Shah said. {115-C13}

quote.text: A fi­nan­cial cen­tre is peo­ple. It is con­ver­sa­tions over cof­fee that is a fi­nan­cial cen­tre.

sections.label: The lessons
sections.head: Feeling for the stones
sections.caption: humility and checks and balances
body: Ajay Shah ad­mit­ted he fought the book page by page. “Look, I was stupid,” he said. Scott is not propos­ing that the state wither away. His mes­sage is hu­mil­ity.

We need a state, Shah said: a mo­nop­oly of vi­o­lence, law and order, mon­e­tary pol­icy. But co­er­cive power should be used with the great­est care. Vijay Kelkar and Shah’s own book has a chap­ter ti­tled after Deng Xiaoping’s “Cross the River by Feeling the Stones”. {115-J17}
Make small moves, things you can undo, Shah said. Scott has a foot­note giv­ing this as one of the many rea­sons he has for op­pos­ing the death penalty. {#deathpenalty}
## Match the sys­tem to the coun­try
“The state spreads its hands in cease­less striv­ing for more ar­bi­trary power,” Shah said, and that striv­ing must be met with com­men­su­rate checks and bal­ances. {115-C14}

His yard­stick is the Freedom House rank­ing, from Norway at the top to North Korea at the bot­tom. Medical records held by the state are fine in the UK, he said, but not in India. “So cer­tain sys­tems should not be in cer­tain coun­tries.” {115-C15}

~ The same hu­mil­ity ar­gues for de­cen­tral­i­sa­tion. India cov­ers 3.3 mil­lion square kilo­me­tres; every func­tion, Shah said, be­longs at the low­est level of gov­ern­ment that can do it. Solving mass trans­port in Bombay is Bombay ex­per­tise.

quote.text: Every func­tion of gov­ern­ment should be done at the low­est level of gov­ern­ment at which it can pos­si­bly be done.
Many short-termist peo­ple see that last mile that one run­ner gets across the race and they say, Yay. But you have to see all the peo­ple that handed the baton up­stream.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Shelves, sparrows, giants and a stage play: the tales that carried the argument

stories.kicker: How Ajay Shah came, at last, to James C Scott
stories.head: The book that waited eight years
body: *Seeing Like a State* came out in 1998, and Ajay Shah missed it com­pletely. Brad DeLong had writ­ten about it on his blog, which was in Shah’s RSS feed, but he failed to catch it there. {115-R04}

Some years later, around 2004 as he re­calls, after the UPA gov­ern­ment came to power, Lant Pritchett moved to Delhi. He gave Shah the book, with Chester Barnard’s *The Functions of the Executive*, and said it would change the way he thought about the world. {115-R05}
“I’m ex­tremely em­bar­rassed to say to you, I did not read it for a long time,” Shah said. From 2004 to 2012, it sat on his shelf. {#sat}

He had com­fort for lis­ten­ers in the same po­si­tion. “Gentle reader, don’t beat your­self up too much be­cause there are all these great books sit­ting on your shelf,” he said. “Our books are our com­pan­ions.” Their phys­i­cal pres­ence, he ar­gued, shapes the day you fi­nally pull one out. {115-S01}
When that day came, he was blown away. He had been, he said, “a cal­low fool” back then, and page after page felt like an as­sault on him.
He fought back, ar­gu­ing with Scott as he read; the book, he said, was un­put­down­able. He blew away all his meet­ings and spent a cou­ple of days doing noth­ing but read­ing the book.
~ Much later in the episode, he put it more vividly: page after page, Scott was slap­ping him in the face.
stories.why: An un­read book on the shelf is not a fail­ure, Shah sug­gested: it waits for its day. And the books that change you most may be the ones you argue with, page after page.
stories.postscript: Amit Varma praised him for chang­ing his mind: most peo­ple, he said, get os­si­fied once their view of the world seems to ex­plain ev­ery­thing.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the book on his shelf

stories.kicker: Amit Varma recalls a war on birds, and its sequel
stories.head: No sparrows, no harvest
body: Ajay Shah had just fin­ished tak­ing apart sci­en­tific forestry when Amit Varma, “a big fan of an­giosperms”, re­called a story about Mao’s high mod­ernism that the hosts had dis­cussed in an ear­lier episode.
Mao, he said, de­cided that all spar­rows should be put to death, be­cause they were harm­ing crops.
But spar­rows ate lo­custs. “Locusts pro­lif­er­ated after spar­rows were killed and ac­tu­ally de­stroyed all the crops and mil­lions of peo­ple starved to death,” Varma said. {115-S05}

~ Shah had just de­scribed a for­est as many species, richly in­ter­con­nected in a web of life, all sym­bi­otic upon each other. {115-C10} Mao pulled out one thread, and the web gave way. There are many such ex­am­ples, Varma added, from all across the world and from India, sadly.
stories.why: A top-down scheme built on one sim­ple the­ory can upset a web no­body fully sees. Locusts fol­lowed spar­rows, famine fol­lowed lo­custs: the costs of high mod­ernism can ar­rive far from where the order was given.

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the petty origin of a gracious line
stories.head: A chip on Newton’s shoulder
body: Amit Varma thought of a quote, we all stand on the shoul­ders of gi­ants, and then of an­other: he couldn’t get any­where be­cause gi­ants were stand­ing on his shoul­der.

Ajay Shah sup­plied the his­tory. The orig­i­nal line, about see­ing fur­ther than oth­ers by stand­ing on the shoul­ders of gi­ants, is Newton’s. “Newton was a truly mean and un­pleas­ant per­son,” he said. {115-S02}
Newton had a life­long ri­valry with Robert Hooke, who was a hunch­back, and who had im­plied that Newton’s ideas were built out of his own work. The fa­mous line was Newton’s put-down.

~ So, Varma asked, how could Shah, a nice guy, be a great thinker? “They are or­thog­o­nal,” Shah replied, and of­fered a Unix for­tune in­stead: “in com­puter sci­ence we stand on each other’s shoul­ders.” {115-J13}

quote.text: The great man Newton was not a nice per­son.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) on Newton and Hooke, with Amit Varma

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s abandoned college play, and its hidden target
stories.head: A ruler in Nehru’s clothing
body: At eigh­teen or nine­teen, Amit Varma and a col­lege friend tried to stage Girish Karnad’s *Tughlaq* as a two-man play.
It never hap­pened. “Inevitably one of us was Bengali and hint it wasn’t him,” Varma said. “And there­fore the project went to hell and I pro­cras­ti­nated.” {115-J10}

Tughlaq, he ex­plained, was a high mod­ernist who shifted his cap­i­tal and did things to the cur­rency, and all of it failed. Karnad wrote the play in the mid-sixties, as dis­il­lu­sion­ment with Nehruvian so­cial­ism set in. So the play was about Nehru too. {115-S08}

~ Varma did not know if Tughlaq was a great man, but Nehru cer­tainly was, as Ajay Shah has said. Shah is com­fort­able sep­a­rat­ing art and artist: Nehru, in his words, was a great artist whose art “was like pretty bad in some ways”. {115-J07}

quote.text: This shows that peo­ple con­tain mul­ti­tudes. Great fol­lies can be made by great men.

stories.postscript: Varma re­gret­ted that *Tughlaq* was his only fic­tion pick, and promised more fic­tion, art and cin­ema from the next episode.

quiz.a: The Velvet Underground: only thirty bought its al­bums, and all be­came mu­si­cians.

quiz.q: Who gave Ajay Shah the book around 2004, and when did he finally read it?
quiz.a: Lant Pritchett, after mov­ing to Delhi; Shah read it only in 2012.

quiz.q: What single purpose does scientific forestry assign to a forest, according to Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: Timber: the most cubic me­tres a year, from one species in rows.

quiz.q: Which four things together, in Scott’s test, produce absolutely bad outcomes?
quiz.a: High mod­ernism, state leg­i­bil­ity, an au­thor­i­tar­ian state and a weak civil so­ci­ety.

quiz.q: Which Greek word did Scott bring into English, and what does it mean?
quiz.a: Metis: deep, local, ex­pe­ri­en­tial knowl­edge that can­not be writ­ten down in a book.

quiz.q: Why does Ajay Shah now say India built Aadhaar in the wrong order?
quiz.a: The pri­vacy law should have come first, be­fore the first num­ber in 2009.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 115. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Isaac Newton (Godfrey Kneller, public domain); James C. Scott (SOAS University of London, CC BY 3.0); Joseph Stalin (Ivan Shagin, public domain); Jane Jacobs (Phil Stanziola, public domain); Robert Caro (Larry D. Moore, CC BY 4.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: Seeing Like a State: How Certain Schemes to Improve the Human Condition Have Failed
shelf.creator: James C Scott
shelf.why: Scott’s ac­count of how state schemes to im­prove the human con­di­tion fail when bu­reau­cra­cies can­not ‘see’ the so­ci­ety they rule, with a tool­kit (state leg­i­bil­ity, high mod­ernism, metis) you can apply al­most any­where.

shelf.title: The Velvet Underground
shelf.creator: The Velvet Underground
shelf.why: The band is a model for James C Scott: lit­tle known to the pub­lic, but hugely in­flu­en­tial on the peo­ple who go on to in­flu­ence ev­ery­one else.

shelf.title: The Long Road to Change (Ep 36 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ the­ory of change: pol­icy im­proves through a decades-long pipe­line of data, re­search, rival pro­pos­als, pub­lic de­bate, com­mit­tee re­ports and draft laws, not by whis­per­ing in a joint secretary’s ear.

shelf.title: Forests, Trees, and Intellectual Roots (review of Seeing Like a State)
shelf.creator: Brad DeLong
shelf.why: An economist’s en­gage­ment with the book, and the place where Ajay could have dis­cov­ered it first.

shelf.title: The Functions of the Executive
shelf.creator: Chester Barnard
shelf.why: Chester Barnard’s book opened Ajay’s think­ing on or­gan­i­sa­tional be­hav­iour and on what goes wrong in large, com­plex or­gan­i­sa­tions, firms and gov­ern­ments alike.

shelf.title: Accidental Politicians (Ep 108 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: In that episode Ajay talked about his ad­mi­ra­tion for Nehru, the back­ground to his point about sep­a­rat­ing the art from the artist.

shelf.title: Metrics for Intervention (Ep 101 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Four met­rics (dis­cre­tion, num­ber of trans­ac­tions, stakes and trans­parency) for judg­ing how hard a job is for the state, which ex­plain why bu­reau­cra­cies strug­gle to see the world ac­cu­rately and why fi­nance is among the hard­est areas to reg­u­late well.

shelf.title: The Problem With Digital Public Goods (Ep 56 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A cri­tique of ‘dig­i­tal pub­lic infrastructure’ such as Aadhaar and UPI: state-backed mo­nop­o­lies cre­ated by co­er­cive power, with­out checks and bal­ances, that crowd out com­pet­ing pri­vate sys­tems.

shelf.title: A Passion for Cycling (Ep 53 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit’s pas­sion for pro­fes­sional cy­cling, which he says will re­main ‘the great­est sport on earth’ even when au­ton­o­mous cars take over, be­cause human en­deav­our, char­ac­ter and dif­fi­culty don’t go away.

shelf.title: Freedom House country scores
shelf.creator: Freedom House
shelf.why: Freedom House’s democ­racy rank­ings, from Norway at the top to North Korea at the bot­tom: a de­cent, easy-to-use mea­sure.

shelf.title: India Needs Decentralization (Ep 47 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The case for sub­sidiar­ity in a coun­try as large and var­ied as India: do as lit­tle as pos­si­ble at the Union level and push power down to cities, where peo­ple can see and talk to the of­fi­cials re­spon­si­ble for their side­walks.

shelf.title: From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Ep 37 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: How Indian firms moved from re­gional satraps in the 1980s to top-down ‘imperial’ firms with uni­form best prac­tices, and then to ‘adaptive’ firms that pair rules with local flex­i­bil­ity.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: The Power Broker
shelf.creator: Robert A Caro
shelf.why: Caro’s mas­ter­piece works on three lev­els: a bi­og­ra­phy of Robert Moses, a bi­og­ra­phy of New York re­shaped by top-down plan­ning, and a study of how power cor­rupts an ide­al­is­tic man.

shelf.title: The Death and Life of Great American Cities
shelf.creator: Jane Jacobs
shelf.why: Jane Jacobs’s ar­gu­ment that cities are about peo­ple, not build­ings and high­ways, and grow or­gan­i­cally from the bot­tom up: spon­ta­neous order and metis against Robert Moses’s high mod­ernism.

shelf.title: Order Without Design
shelf.creator: Alain Bertaud
shelf.why: Amit’s desert-island book on cities: Bertaud brings eco­nom­ics and many other dis­ci­plines to urban plan­ning, ex­poses the fol­lies of high mod­ernism and re­spects the local knowl­edge be­hind why streets and cities work as they do.

shelf.title: The Hidden Life of Trees
shelf.creator: Peter Wohlleben
shelf.why: It shows that a nat­u­ral for­est is a com­mu­ni­cat­ing sys­tem, with roots talk­ing to each other and trees ad­just­ing when one is harmed.

shelf.title: Tughlaq
shelf.creator: Girish Karnad
shelf.why: A play about a ruler whose grand schemes failed, writ­ten in the mid-sixties as a veiled com­ment on Nehruvian so­cial­ism.

laughs.text: Amit: ‘We all stand on the shoul­ders of gi­ants. And the other quote... is that I couldn’t get any­where be­cause gi­ants was stand­ing on my shoul­der.’

Ajay’s EIE T-shirt line: vol­ume one, num­ber one is ‘Make trade not war’, and num­ber two is ‘State leg­i­bil­ity schemes have un­in­tended consequences’. Amit replies that you could only buy it in triple XL, ‘be­cause how will the words fit?’
Amit: ‘When I first heard the phrase high mod­ernism, I thought it ba­si­cally means that you wear shirt pant and you do drugs.’
Amit on how con­fus­ingly sim­i­lar ‘modernity’ and ‘high modernism’ sound: ‘It’s like pop­u­lar­ity and pop­ulism... They’re al­most op­po­site things.’
Ajay on the mis­use of ‘scientific’ in pol­icy: ‘So I get of­fended when any­body says sci­en­tific. I’m like dude don’t pull the sci­ence card on me.’
On his failed col­lege stag­ing of Tughlaq: ‘in­evitably one of us was Bengali and hint it wasn’t him. And there­fore the project went to hell and I pro­cras­ti­nated.’
Amit re­minds Ajay he once promised seven rec­om­men­da­tions and then gave none. Ajay: ‘In the next episode I will give you nine rec­om­men­da­tions.’

Amit calls James C Scott ‘the Velvet Underground of ideas’, after the line that only thirty peo­ple bought the band’s al­bums and all thirty be­came mu­si­cians. He adds that the Velvet Revolution was named after the band.
A Unix for­tune Ajay quotes as a coun­ter­point to Newton: ‘in com­puter sci­ence we stand on each other’s shoul­ders.’
Ajay on sci­en­tific forestry: ‘ex­plain­ing a joke is like dis­sect­ing a frog. You can un­der­stand it, but it kills the frog.’ Imposing leg­i­bil­ity killed the for­est in the same way.
Deng Xiaoping’s ‘Cross the River by Feeling the Stones’, a chap­ter title in Kelkar and Shah’s book, used as short­hand for Scott’s ad­vice to make small, re­versible moves.
